clue.text: Prices here are lower — but literally so?

definitions.text: Prices here are lower — but literally so?

parts.words: Prices here are lower — but literally so
parts.note: cheap goods are sold here, and the sales floor is literally lower too, being below ground level

explanation.surface: A remark about a shop section where things cost less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' works twice: lower prices, and a floor physically below street level in a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: The cut-price section of a store, traditionally on its underground floor, sells reduced goods.

clue.text: Spy chief in resolving mystery shows proportion

indicators.note: the spymaster's letter is set within the rearranged word
resolving a puzzle means working it out, so the letters of mystery are reworked

parts.note: M is the head of the secret service in the James Bond stories

explanation.surface: An intelligence boss unravelling a puzzle displays a sense of balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spy chief' looks like the first letter of Spy, but it is M from Bond; 'resolving' rearranges MYSTERY around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Balanced correspondence of parts, as in a well-made shape, is a synonym for proportion.

clue.text: Client American employer cleaned out

indicators.note: emptying the word employer of its middle leaves only its outside letters

explanation.surface: A US company boss has been left broke by a customer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who uses a service or product is its customer, a sense close to client.

clue.text: Heads off for winter in pet surfing place

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the three words winter, in and pet is removed

explanation.surface: A seasonal instruction about where to keep an animal during cold months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads off' removes W, I and P from the three words, leaving INTER, N and ET.
explanation.definitionFit: People browse websites, called surfing the web, on the global computer network.

clue.text: Gossip and joke about capsized sailors

indicators.note: the joke word goes around the sailors

parts.note: a gag is a joke

indicators.note: in a down clue, a boat turning over turns the word for sailors upside down

parts.note: ABs are able seamen

explanation.surface: Chatter and humour about some sailors whose boat has overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' suits a down clue, where the sailors' word is read upward; 'about' wraps the joke around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who talks too much, a chatterbox, is called a windbag or a gossip.

clue.text: Principal villain lacking vertical 2?

parts.note: top means leading or principal
the heavy is the villain in a play or film

explanation.surface: A lead baddie with an odd structural flaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 refers to the answer at 2-down, SYMMETRY: something too weighty above is unbalanced from top to bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: An object with too much weight up high is unbalanced along its upright axis.

clue.text: Big prawns swindle — one pockets penny

indicators.note: the swindle with one added takes the coin into its middle, as a pocket holds money

parts.note: a scam is a swindle
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A seafood fraud in which someone keeps a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway lobsters, also called Dublin Bay prawns, are large prawn-like shellfish served breaded.

clue.text: Some people in queer street do big shop

indicators.note: the two words sit inside the rearranged letters
queer in its old sense of odd signals that street and do are scrambled

parts.note: part means some of something
men means people

explanation.surface: Folk who are broke still go on a large shopping trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Queer Street' is an old British idiom for being in debt; the surface hides that 'queer' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A large retail store divided into sections selling many kinds of goods is a big shop.

clue.text: Where Selassie ruled we'll meet again, as you might say!

indicators.note: signals that the farewell phrase spoken casually gives the answer's sound

parts.note: a farewell like 'I'll be seeing ya'

explanation.surface: A goodbye promising another meeting, with a nod to an emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: A casual 'I'll be seein' ya' is pronounced like the old country name.
explanation.definitionFit: Haile Selassie was emperor of Ethiopia, formerly known by this older name.

clue.text: Person brings in copper at the right moment

indicators.note: the person word takes the copper symbol inside it

parts.note: one means a person, as in 'one should'
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Someone fetches a police officer at just the right time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is the chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor entering exactly when signalled is punctual; the idiom means at exactly the right time.

clue.text: Difficult or sticky situation encountered up here?

definitions.text: Difficult or sticky situation encountered up here?

parts.words: Difficult or sticky situation encountered up here
parts.note: the idiom 'up a eucalyptus' means in trouble, and the tree exudes sticky gum

explanation.surface: A question about where one finds oneself in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up a gum tree' is a British idiom for being in difficulties; 'sticky' doubles as gummy.
explanation.definitionFit: A eucalyptus exudes resin, and the idiom places someone in trouble up one.

clue.text: Round with half consumed by graduate in Czech region

indicators.note: the round and half are eaten up inside the graduate letters

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts
O is round in shape
hemi- is the prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: A graduate swallowing a round and a half in a Czech region, perhaps of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The western part of the Czech Republic around Prague is this historic kingdom.

clue.text: Letter from Eliot analysed

indicators.note: the letters are taken from within the words Eliot analysed

explanation.surface: A letter written by T.S. Eliot that someone has studied.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth character of the Greek alphabet, so a letter.

clue.text: I set puzzle — am I setting cryptically?

indicators.note: in a cryptic manner, so the letters of am I setting are rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter wonders whether they are writing crosswords obscurely.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter of riddles or puzzles describes themselves as I set puzzles.

clue.text: Cricketer puts lad to bed, quiet at last

parts.note: a boy is a lad
a cot is a child's bed

indicators.note: only the final letter of quiet is used

explanation.surface: A sportsman settles a child for the night and finally it is calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Geoffrey Boycott was a famous Yorkshire and England batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Geoffrey Boycott was an England opening batsman, so an example of a cricketer.

clue.text: Dutiful bit done badly involves leader in embarrassment

indicators.note: the rearranged letters enclose the leading letter
done badly means the letters of bit done are put in a poor order
takes the first letter of embarrassment

explanation.surface: A job poorly done that causes some embarrassment for the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges BIT DONE; 'involves' puts E inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone compliant and doing as told is dutiful.

clue.text: Free drug taken by girl for jaunt in stolen car

indicators.note: the free-and-drug pair comes after the girl's name

parts.note: Joy is a girl's name
rid means free, as in get rid of
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A girl takes a free drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckless drive in a car taken without permission, for thrills, is this.

clue.text: Sportsman scrutinised and deviously manipulated

parts.note: a jock is an athletic man, a sports enthusiast
eyed means looked at closely

explanation.surface: A sportsman was studied and then cunningly manoeuvred.
explanation.definitionFit: Manoeuvring craftily for advantage is the verb, as riders jostle for position.

clue.text: Edmund II to press on border

indicators.note: in a down clue, the press word sits on top of the border word

parts.note: to iron is to press clothes
a side is an edge or border

explanation.surface: An instruction to press along an edge, perhaps of a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund II was an English king of 1016, known by this nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The English king Edmund II bore this epithet for his strength in battle.

clue.text: Money and support for big ape

parts.note: silver means coins, money
to back is to support

explanation.surface: Cash and backing for a large primate, like a fundraiser for gorillas.
explanation.definitionFit: A mature male gorilla, with grey hair on its rear, is a large ape.

clue.text: Friendless new driver covering Fenland location

parts.note: L for learner, shown on L-plates
on means covering, as a lid sits on a jar
Ely is a cathedral city in the Cambridgeshire Fens

explanation.surface: A solitary learner driving across the flat Fens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are low marshy farmland in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without companions or friends makes one isolated and sad.

clue.text: Where one may see patient escape madhouse

parts.note: a hospital patient lies in a bed
lam is US slang for escape, as in on the lam

explanation.surface: A patient escaping from an asylum.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedlam was the old name of a London asylum.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene of uproar and chaos, from the old Bethlem asylum, is a madhouse.

clue.text: Shilling in purse constitutes stake

indicators.note: the shilling letter sits inside the purse word

parts.note: the pot is the money wagered, the prize purse
S is the abbreviation for the old British shilling

explanation.surface: A shilling placed in a prize pot makes a bet.
explanation.walkthrough: The shilling was a pre-1971 British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A pole driven into the ground is a stake.

clue.text: Exotic mink and sentient apes?

indicators.note: exotic means strange or foreign, signalling the letters of mink and are altered

explanation.surface: Unusual furry animals alongside thinking primates.
explanation.definitionFit: The human race, cheekily described as thinking primates.

clue.text: Clearly demonstrate power over sons in retirement

indicators.note: the three letters sit inside the retirement word

parts.note: an exit is a departure, a retirement from a stage
P is the symbol for power
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Showing how power passes to the sons when the father retires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' looks like a reversal signal but is EXIT, a withdrawal.
explanation.definitionFit: To set forth or expound clearly is to demonstrate plainly.

clue.text: Papa with fish to commune with deity

parts.note: P is papa in the NATO alphabet
a ray is a flat fish

explanation.surface: A father fishing as a form of worship.
explanation.definitionFit: Addressing God in prayer is communing with the divine.

clue.text: Only played with new material

indicators.note: played with, toyed with, so the letters of only are moved about

explanation.surface: Only fiddling with some new fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic polymer fibre used in stockings and fabric is a material.

clue.text: Great man admits unknown to Ace Rowing Club

parts.note: A is the card ace

indicators.note: the rowing club letters let the unknown in

parts.note: Leander is a famous rowing club at Henley-on-Thames
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A distinguished man joins a rowing club.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander Club is the elite British rowing club at Henley.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great, the Macedonian conqueror, was this great man.
